The Eastern meadowlark (Sturnella magna) is a ground-nesting icterid that breeds across grasslands and pastures of eastern North America. Eggs are incubated by the female for a period averaging 13.5 days [ab = 13.5 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration typical for passerines of this body size. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on parental care and weigh a mere 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams], representing an extremely small fraction of the adult female's ultimate body mass. This low hatchling weight reflects the substantial energetic investment required for incubation and the subsequent rapid growth phase necessary for fledging within a short nestling period.

Under the elevated metabolic conditions typical of the active breeding season (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the nestling developmental schedule is relatively compressed. Fledging, defined as the age at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight, occurs at 11 days after hatching [tx = 11 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid development is accompanied by a progressive increase in body mass. The ultimate wet weight for adult females of the nominate subspecies Sturnella magna magna has been recorded at 112 grams [Wwi = 112 grams], a figure that represents the maximum asymptotic mass these birds attain and which is reached only after the completion of post-fledging growth and the acquisition of full adult plumage during the first winter.

Sexual maturation in the Eastern meadowlark follows a trajectory that is partially decoupled from the rapid early growth phase. Puberty, measured as the age at which gonadal development is sufficiently advanced to enable reproductive function, is attained at 33 days after hatching [tp = 33 days after hatching], again assessed at a body temperature of 41.6 °C at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. It is important to note, however, that this physiological readiness does not immediately translate into reproductive activity. While the gonads may be mature, young birds typically delay their first breeding efforts, channeling resources instead into establishing territories and building body condition, a common life-history strategy among altricial songbirds.

First reproduction, or the age at which an individual completes its first successful brood, occurs considerably later than puberty would suggest. Field records indicate that females initiate their first brood at approximately 10.5 months after hatching [tR = approximately 10.5 months after hatching], which equates to the early breeding season of the following calendar year, when measured under the standard field metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This substantial delay, spanning from fledging in summer to the next spring, is a period largely dedicated to overwinter survival, territory acquisition, and the completion of structural growth. Once a female begins breeding, she typically produces two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], each containing a maximum of 6 eggs [N_R_i = each containing a maximum of 6 eggs], yielding a high potential reproductive output for a monogamous grassland bird.

Longevity data for the Eastern meadowlark reveal a lifespan that is modest relative to the species' reproductive potential. The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild reaches 12.6 years [am = 12.6 years], a figure that reflects the cumulative mortality risks associated with grassland habitats, including predation, agricultural machinery, and severe winter weather, when assessed under the standard metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short average lifespan in the wild, compared to some other icterids of similar size, is counterbalanced by the species' high annual fecundity, achieved through the combination of large clutch sizes and multiple breeding attempts per season. The trade-off between early reproduction and longevity is a classic feature of the life history of this open-country specialist.
